title: Call Him by His names
hook: the beautiful names again, in their home verse (7:180)

segments.voice: Yesterday: mithaq, the covenant of Alast. Your line was we said yes. Today, the beautiful names come back, in the verse they call home.

On day two hundred thirty-two, this path opened the most beautiful names of Allah with the first half of this verse: the Merciful, the Forgiving, the Provider, the Patient. Lists of names are lovely to read, and easy to treat like a museum, beautiful things behind glass. Today, the verse again, read all the way through, in its place in surah seven. It says what the names are for, and then how they can be bent.
screen: `DAY 232, THE FIRST HALF.` → `NAMES BEHIND GLASS?` → `WHAT THEY'RE FOR.`

segments.voice: Verse one-eighty, in Pickthall's words: “Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them.” In Arabic: wa lillahi al-asma' al-husna, fad'uhu biha. The word for call, ud'u, shares a root with du'a. The names aren't only to know. They're to use, the way you use someone's name to get their attention. So scholars teach matching the name to the need: when you need provision, ar-Razzaq, the Provider; when you've done wrong, al-Ghafur, the Forgiving; when you're afraid, as-Salam, Peace. The verse goes on: leave those who distort His names. The verb is yulhiduna, from a root meaning to swerve to one side. A Muslim grave may have a lahd, a niche dug into the side wall: the same root. To distort the names is to bend them away from what they mean. How many are there? A hadith in Bukhari says Allah has ninety-nine names, and whoever counts them will enter paradise; scholars explained count as learning, understanding and living by them. But some scholars held that ninety-nine is not the limit, citing a du'a reported from the Prophet ﷺ that asks by every name Allah has named Himself, including those He kept hidden with Himself. The list is a door, not the whole house. The phrase al-asma' al-husna appears in four places in the Qur'an. Here it comes with a plain command, and a warning.
screen: `FAD'UHU BIHA — CALL ON HIM BY THEM.` · `MATCH THE NAME TO THE NEED.` · `ILHAD — TO SWERVE ASIDE.` · `NINETY-NINE, AND MORE.` · then, large: `THE NAMES ARE FOR CALLING.`

segments.voice: Name to yourself one thing you need today, plainly: patience with a child, money for rent, courage for a conversation, rest. Pick the name that fits it, the Patient, the Provider, the Strong, Peace. If you pray, call on Him by that name quietly, a few times with the breath; if you don't, sit with the name and the need side by side.
Al-asma' al-husna, the most beautiful names. Surah seven, verse one-eighty: to Allah belong them, so call on Him by them.
Your line: the names are for calling. Each one fits a need. Day four hundred fourteen, done.

howItsDone: Muslims often begin a du'a with the divine name that fits the request, such as ya Razzaq for provision or ya Ghafur for forgiveness, and some learn the ninety-nine names by heart.

what a scholar hears: al-asma' al-husna appears in 7:180, 17:110, 20:8 and 59:24; Ibn Mas'ud's reported du'a (Musnad Ahmad) asks by names 'kept in the unseen', so scholars such as al-Nawawi held the names are not limited to ninety-nine.

options: Not only: 7:180 says call on Him by them. Match the name to the need, like the Provider for rent.
Yes, they're for reciting in order; using one in a personal request is disrespectful.
They're titles for the Prophet, praising him, and 7:180 asks people to learn them.
